query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin niobium (Nb) interlayer between the HEA layers increases interface coherency such that the dominant creep mechanism shifts from a diffusion-mediated mode to a dislocation-mediated mode at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers with coherent interfaces and primarily diffusion-mediated creep behavior under high-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Insertion of an ultrathin, adjustable-thickness refractory Nb interlayer into the HEA multilayer stack.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep testing (approximately 600–700 °C) under controlled applied stress; conditions where both diffusion and dislocation creep mechanisms could be active.
generation.structural_mediator: The Nb interlayer, with its intermediate lattice parameter relative to the adjacent HEA layers, mediates the interface coherency, reducing lattice mismatch and modifying local strain fields.
generation.mechanism: By adjusting the Nb layer thickness, the activation energy for diffusion is increased through enhanced coherency, thereby suppressing vacancy diffusion (and thus diffusion-mediated creep) while facilitating dislocation glide or climb. This transition results from the interface’s modified atomic bonding state and lattice matching.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in the creep rate associated with diffusion-dominated deformation and the emergence of dislocation-mediated slip mechanisms, observable by comparing microstructural features (e.g., dislocation densities and slip band formation) between samples with and without the Nb interlayer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers lacking the Nb interlayer, which under similar high-temperature stress conditions primarily exhibit diffusion-mediated creep behavior.
generation.boundary: The beneficial influence of the Nb interlayer may depend on its precise thickness and processing conditions; excessive thickness or degradation of interface coherency at temperatures beyond the tested range could negate the intended effect.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative shift in activation energies and the optimal Nb interlayer thickness for achieving the transition remain to be precisely determined through systematic experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set incorporating an ultrathin, adjustable-thickness Nb interlayer and a control set without the Nb interlayer. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature creep tests under controlled stress. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM), creep rate measurements, and activation energy calculations to assess the deformation mechanisms.
measurements: Creep rate (strain vs. time) under high-temperature conditions
Stress exponent and activation energy values derived from mechanical tests
Microstructural analysis (TEM) to identify the presence and predominance of dislocation structures versus diffusion-based features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Nb interlayer do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in diffusion-mediated creep rates or lack evidence of enhanced dislocation-mediated mechanisms (compared to the control samples), then the hypothesis that the Nb interlayer facilitates the transition will be falsified.

At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. frame.system: High‐entropy alloy multilayers used as advanced coatings, where alternating layers form coherent interfaces.
frame.goal: To identify and explain a candidate material that, when used as an interlayer or transition layer, enables the shift from diffusion‐mediated to dislocation‐mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
frame.limitation: The precise impact of interface coherency on creep behavior in these HEA multilayers is not yet understood.
root_cause_cues: interface coherency on the creep behavior remains unclear
transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
constraints: The candidate material must be compatible with the overall high-entropy system
It needs to provide an intermediate lattice parameter or bonding state that can bridge the coherency of adjoining layers
It should influence the activation energies such that diffusion processes can give way to dislocation-based deformation under appropriate temperature and stress conditions
frame.regime: High-temperature creep conditions where both diffusion (e.g. Coble or Nabarro–Herring creep) and dislocation mechanisms are active and their competition is sensitive to interface structure.
prior_attempts: Prior work on HEA multilayers has demonstrated excellent mechanical and irradiation properties, but these studies did not isolate the role of interface coherency on the steady-state creep mechanism.
Similar multilayer systems (e.g. Cu/Nb systems) have been explored, yet they fell short in clarifying how a controlled transition layer could switch the dominant creep mechanism.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in high‐entropy systems have primarily focused on establishing bulk and coating properties – such as strength, oxidation resistance and ductility – via advanced processing routes (laser cladding, HPHT treatment, additive manufacturing). In several cases (e.g., PMC11087546), the work highlighted that achieving highly coherent interfaces (low lattice mismatch) can dramatically influence deformation behavior. Yet, while such processing has improved overall mechanical performance, none have directly isolated or engineered an interfacial transition layer to trigger a controlled switch between diffusion‐mediated (e.g. Coble or Nabarro–Herring creep) and dislocation‐mediated creep. In parallel, studies on related multilayer systems (like Cu/Nb) hinted at the potential of introducing an intermediate layer to tune the activation energies of competing creep mechanisms, but this idea has not been expressly transferred to HEA multilayers.
decision.unsolved: The open question remains how to design an interlayer with just the right lattice parameter and bonding state such that its coherent interface with the HEA layers can mediate the transition from diffusion‐dominated creep (effective at very high temperatures) to dislocation‐dominated creep, particularly under high-temperature service conditions.
decision.lever: Introduce a thin, refractory Nb interlayer with adjustable thickness as a transition material within the HEA multilayer stack
decision.why: Niobium has a lattice parameter intermediate between many refractory HEAs and is already compatible within such systems. By systematically varying the Nb layer thickness and interface coherency via controlled deposition, one can tailor the activation energies at the interfaces to diminish diffusion‐mediated creep and favor dislocation-mediated mechanisms – a natural extension of previous work on coherent interfaces in HEA coatings and multilayers.

families.best_lever: Conduct atomistic simulations (e.g., molecular dynamics with accelerated sampling) to characterize the interplay between interface structure and activation energies governing the creep transition.

families.principle: Systematically varying the interlayer material properties (e.g., lattice parameter, bonding state) to measure the resulting changes in creep behavior and isolate the transition mechanism.

impact of interface coherency on the creep behavior

families.best_lever: Design experiments with graded interlayers that vary slightly in lattice parameter to bridge the coherency, then measure activation energy variations under high-temperature creep.
